analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary public financing system for Senate campaigns and bans unlimited party 'soft money'.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 1997 with 3 Senate sponsors, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee the same day, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Senate candidates opt into a system where they agree to strict spending limits and stop taking general-election donations, in exchange for public campaign funds from a new Congressional Election Campaign Fund. It would cut the ceiling on PAC donations to Senate campaigns from $5,000 to $2,000, ban national and state party committees from raising or spending unregulated 'soft money', and bar campaign contributions from people who cannot legally vote, including foreign nationals. The money would come voluntarily: taxpayers could check a box sending $10 to election funds ($3 presidential, $7 congressional) and could add up to $5,000 more, with a small tax deduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates who agree to the limits — especially challengers without access to big donors — would receive full public financing for their campaigns. Voters would get elections in which candidates are not funded by large checks from PACs, wealthy individuals, and party soft-money networks, and candidates' own family fortunes would be capped at $10,000 for participating campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates without big donors

how_it_helps.text: A Senate candidate who agrees to spending caps (roughly $5.5 million for a general election, scaled by state population and higher rates for states with only one TV station) would receive public payments covering that full amount from the new fund.
Participating candidates could take no general-election contributions at all and could contribute at most $10,000 of their own or their family's money to their campaign.

National and state party committees would be barred from soliciting, receiving, or spending any money outside the limits and reporting rules of federal campaign law, and from funneling money to tax-exempt 501(c) organizations.
PAC contributions to Senate campaigns would be cut from $5,000 to $2,000 per election.

If outside groups or non-participating opponents outspend a participating candidate, the candidate's limit would rise — up to 100% higher against a big-spending opponent — and independent spending by outside groups would trigger matching amounts, with 24-hour public reporting of such spending.
Individuals not qualified to register to vote in federal elections, including foreign nationals, would be barred from contributing to federal campaigns.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers who choose to participate: the fund is filled by a voluntary $10 income-tax checkoff ($3 to presidential elections, $7 to congressional) and optional extra contributions of $1 to $5,000, with a deduction capped at $100 per person. If the checkoff money falls short of what participating candidates are owed, the bill authorizes appropriations to cover the gap. Candidates who want to spend more than the caps simply forgo public funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers who opt in to checkoff

drawbacks.text: The spending limits at the heart of the bill apply to candidates' own campaign speech; in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) the Supreme Court struck down mandatory limits of this kind as a First Amendment problem, so the core design faced serious constitutional doubt — the bill manages this only by making participation voluntary.

Because the system is voluntary, a candidate who opts out faces no real limits: the bill's escalators only lift the participating candidate's cap by 20% to 100% as the opponent spends beyond 110% to 200% of the limit, so a very wealthy self-funder or a heavily funded outsider could still dominate a race.

Public money would flow directly to politicians' campaign accounts, and if voluntary checkoff designations fall short, the bill authorizes general-tax appropriations to make up the difference — a cost critics would call hard to justify while campaigns remain optional.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a real swing at the largest money channels in Senate politics — unlimited soft money, big PAC checks, and self-funding — and pays for it through a voluntary checkoff rather than mandatory taxation, which keeps the direct cost small. Its weaknesses are structural: voluntary spending limits are constitutionally fragile and leave big spenders free to outspend participants, and a candidate can only be held to the caps if enough money exists in the fund. A reasonable design with real costs and real open questions — but the public stakes in reducing money's grip on Senate elections are substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and quietly died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Dale Bumpers introduced the Public Confidence in Campaigns Act of 1997 on January 29, 1997, joined by Sens. Patty Murray and Paul Wellstone.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever recorded on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

The bill would have set Senate campaign spending limits of roughly $5.5 million for a general election (with a population-based formula and a higher per-capita rate for states with only one commercial TV transmitter) in exchange for full public financing from a new Congressional Election Campaign Fund.

It would have banned party soft money, cut PAC contributions to Senate candidates to $2,000, capped participating candidates' personal spending at $10,000, and barred contributions from individuals not qualified to vote.

Funding would have come from a voluntary income-tax checkoff splitting $10 between presidential ($3) and congressional ($7) election funds, plus optional additional contributions of up to $5,000 with a limited tax deduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National and state party committees, large donors, and PACs kept the existing fundraising system untouched — no soft-money ban, no lower PAC limits, no spending caps — and incumbent senators continued running under the rules they already knew.

for.name: Sen. Dale Bumpers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor the day it was filed.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair William Roth)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing or markup — after it was referred on January 29, 1997; the bill died there.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the 105th Senate floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Did not bring campaign finance reform measures to the Senate floor for votes during the 105th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the Finance Committee was chaired by a Republican, but no hearing or vote was ever held, so the record shows no partisan lineup on the bill itself.

industries.note: The bill bans parties from soliciting or spending unlimited, unregulated soft money and from routing funds through 501(c) groups, ending a major fundraising channel. Parties fought to keep that channel, and its survival serves their institutional interest rather than voters'.

Cutting PAC limits for Senate races to $2,000 and replacing general-election donations with public financing shrinks the leverage of big organized money over candidates. The bill's value to ordinary voters lies precisely in reducing that leverage.

Participating candidates could put at most $10,000 of family money into a campaign, but the system is voluntary: a wealthy candidate who opts out faces no limit, only reporting duties and modest escalators for opponents.
